Time Line

Event
Yamasee War. The Yamasee and their allies fight against the English
for trading and other abuses.
Natchez Revolt. Resisting French attempts to exact tribute, the Natchez
go to war; the tribe is essentially destroyed, and many are sold
into slavery.
Articles of Agreement signed between the Cherokee Nation and
King George II.
Russia explores the Alaskan coast and begins trading operations.
Some Iroquois settle near the Catholic mission of St. Regis, forming
the nucleus of the Akwesasne Reserve.
Proclamation of 1763. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 declares that
Native Americans have title to all lands outside established colonies until the Crown legally purchases further land cessions.
Pontiac’s War. Ottawa leader Pontiac constructs a multitribal alliance
to resist the British.
Paxton Riots (Paxton Boys Massacre). On December 14, 1765, seventyfive Europeans from Paxton, Pennsylvania, massacre and scalp
six innocent Conestoga Mission Indians.
Treaty of Fort Stanwix. The Iroquois Confederacy cedes lands south
of the Ohio River (a later Fort Stanwix Treaty, 1784, changes the
agreement).
The California mission system is established.
Labrador Inuit show missionaries where to build a trading post.
Lord Dunmore’s War. Lord Dunmore, the governor of Virginia, leads
a fight against Shawnee led by Cornstalk.
The first Continental Congress establishes an Indian Department.
The Iroquois Confederacy is dispersed by the American Revolution.
Northwest Ordinance. The U.S. Congress establishes a legal mechanism to create states from territories.
The Indian Department becomes part of the U.S. Department of War.
First of the Trade and Intercourse Acts enacted; they attempt to
regulate trade between Europeans and Native Americans.
Little Turtle’s War. Shawnee and their allies under Little Turtle defeat
Anthony St. Clair’s troops in 1791 but eventually are defeated at
the Battle of Fallen Timbers, 1794, by General Anthony Wayne.
Treaty of Fort Greenville. Native Americans of the Old Northwest are
forced to treat with the United States after Britain refuses to assist
them in their resistance efforts.
Trading Houses Act. On April 18, 1796, the United States establishes
government-operated trading houses.
Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet, founds the Gaiwiio, “the Good
Word,” also known as the Longhouse religion; it becomes a strong
force among the Iroquois.
Louisiana Purchase. The United States acquires 800,000 square miles
of new territory.
Lewis and Clark expedition. President Jefferson launches an expedition to collect information of national interest about Louisiana.

American Indian Tribes
Event
Treaty of Fort Wayne. The Delaware are forced to relinquish approximately 3 million acres.
Tecumseh’s Rebellion. Shawnee leader Tecumseh leads a multitribal
force to resist United States incursions into their lands.
Battle of Tippecanoe. William Henry Harrison and his forces attack
and defeat Tecumseh’s forces in Tecumseh’s absence.
War of 1812. Tribes of the Old Northwest are drawn into the European conflict.
In August, the Hudson’s Bay Company establishes the Red River
Colony.
Red Stick civil war. Creeks fight a bloody civil war over disagreements about what their political relations with the United States
should be.
First Seminole War. U.S. forces under General Andrew Jackson attack
and burn Seminole villages.
Sequoyah creates the Cherokee syllabary, the first system for writing
an Indian language.
Johnson v. M’Intosh. On February 28, 1823, the U.S. Supreme Court
rules that Native American tribes have land rights.
Office of Indian Affairs is created within the War Department.
Cherokee Nation adopts a constitution.
Indian Removal Act. At the urging of President Andrew Jackson,
Congress orders the removal of all Native Americans to lands
west of the Mississippi River. Removal proceeds from the 1830’s
to the 1850’s.
Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. Choctaws cede more than 10 million
acres in Alabama and Mississippi.
Upper Canada establishes a system of reserves for Canadian natives.
Cherokee Nation v. Georgia. U.S. Supreme Court rules that Native
American tribes are “domestic dependent nations.”
Black Hawk War. Black Hawk, the Sauk and Fox leader leads a war
to preserve their land rights.
Worcester v. Georgia. U.S. Supreme Court rules that only the federal
government has the right to regulate Indian affairs.
Department of Indian Affairs is reorganized.
Texas Rangers begin raids against the Comanche.
Second Seminole War. The Seminole resist removal to Indian Territory.
Forced removal of Cherokees to Indian Territory becomes a “Trail of
Tears” marked by thousands of deaths.
Upper Canadian Judge James Buchanan submits a report suggesting
that Canadian natives should be assimilated into larger Canadian
society.
Taos Revolt. Taos Pueblos struggle against U.S. domination.
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. United States acquires southwestern
lands from Mexico.

Time Line

Event
California Gold Rush. Emigrants cross Native American lands, resulting in ecological destruction and spread of diseases.
Metis Courthouse Rebellion. Metis resist Canadian domination.
Period of genocide against California Indians begins and continues
for some thirty years; thousands are killed.
First Treaty of Fort Laramie. Great Plains Native Americans agree to
allow emigrants safe passage across their territories.
Gadsden Purchase. U.S. government purchases portions of Arizona,
California, and New Mexico from
Mexico.
Teton Dakota Resistance. The Teton Dakota and their allies resist U.S.
intrusions into their lands.
In the Northwest, Territorial Governor Isaac Stevens holds the Walla
Walla Council and negotiates a series of treaties with Native
American tribes.
Yakima War. Led by Kamiakin, who refused to sign the 1855 treaty,
Yakimas fight U.S. forces after the murder of a government Indian
agent initiates hostilities.
Third Seminole War. Seminoles react to the surveying of their lands.
British Columbia Gold Rush precipitates large-scale invasion of Indian lands.
Navajo War. Manuelito leads the Navajo against U.S. forces to fight
against whites’ grazing their horses on Navajo lands.
The British transfer full responsibility of Canadian Indian affairs to
the Province of Canada.
Minnesota Uprising. Little Crow carries out a war of resistance
against federal authority because of ill treatment.
Long Walk of the Navajo. In a violent campaign, U.S. forces remove
the Navajo from their homeland and take them to Bosque Redondo.
Sand Creek Massacre. Colorado militiamen under John Chivington
massacre a peaceful group of Cheyennes at Sand Creek.
Bozeman Trail wars. Teton Dakota and their allies resist the building
of army forts in their lands.
U.S. government purchases Alaska.
Canadian Confederation. The Dominion of Canada is created.
Commission Act. Legislation calls for the U.S. president to establish
commissions to negotiate peace treaties with Native American
nations.
Second Treaty of Fort Laramie pledges the protection of Indian lands.
Canadian government adopts an Indian policy aimed at the assimilation of Indians into Canadian society.
Washita River Massacre. A peaceful Cheyenne camp is massacred by
the U.S. Seventh Cavalry.
First Riel Rebellion. Louis Reil leads the Metis in resisting Canadian
domination; partly triggered by white surveying of Metis lands.

American Indian Tribes
Event
Grant’s Peace Policy. President Ulysses S. Grant assigns various
Christian denominations to various Indian reservation agencies in
order to Christianize and pacify the Indians.
Congress passes an act on March 3 that ends treaty negotiations with
Native American nations.
McKay v. Campbell. U.S. Supreme Court holds that Indian people
born with “tribal allegiance” are not U.S. citizens.
Canada begins negotiating the first of eleven “numbered” treaties
with Native Canadians.
Wholesale destruction of the bison on the Plains.
Modoc War. The Modoc resist removal to the Klamath Reservation.
Canadian Northwest Mounted Police move to establish order in the
Canadian West.
Red River War. Forced by starvation and Indian agent corruption,
Kiowa, Plains Apache, Southern Cheyenne, and Arapaho raid
European American farms and ranches to feed their families.
First Indian Act of Canada. The act consolidated Canadian policies
toward its indigenous people.
Battle of the Little Bighorn. General Custer and the Seventh Cavalry
are annihilated by the Sioux, Cheyenne, and Arapaho camped
along the Little Bighorn River.
The Nez Perce are exiled from their homeland and pursued by U.S.
forces as they unsuccessfully attempt to escape into Canada.
Battle of Wolf Mountain. The last fight between the Cheyenne and
the U.S. Army.
The Northern Cheyenne are forcibly removed to Indian Territory but
escape north to their homelands.
Bannock War. Because of settler pressures, the Bannock are forced to
raid for food.
Carlisle Indian School, a boarding school with the goal of “civilizing” Indian youth, is founded by Captain Richard H. Pratt.
Canadian officials modify the 1876 Indian Act, empowering it to
impose elected councils on bands.
Second Riel Rebellion. Louis Riel leads a second protest, then armed
revolt, among the Canadian Metis and Cree; defeated, Riel is
executed after the rebellion.
General Allotment Act (Dawes Severalty Act). Provides for the dividing of reservation lands into individual parcels to expedite assimilation. (By the early twentieth century, the allotment policy is
viewed as disastrous.)
Wounded Knee Massacre. The Seventh Cavalry intercepts a group of
Sioux Ghost Dancers being led by Big Foot to the Pine Ridge
Reservation. When a Sioux warrior, perhaps accidentally, fires his
rifle, the army opens fire; hundreds of Sioux, most unarmed, are
massacred.
Education Appropriation Act mandates funding for Indian day
schools and technical schools.

Time Line

Event
Indian Liquor Act bans the sale or distribution of liquor to Native
Americans.
Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock. U.S. Supreme Court rules that Congress has
the authority to dispose of Native American lands.
Burke Act. Congress amends the General Allotment Act to shorten
the trust period for individual Native Americans who are proven
“competent.”
Alaskan Allotment Act. Allows Alaska Natives to file for 160-acre
parcels.
Omnibus Act. Establishes procedures to determine Native American
heirship of trust lands and other resources.
Classification and Appraisal of Unallotted Indian Lands Act. Permits
the Secretary of Interior to reappraise and reclassify unallotted
Indian lands.
General Citizenship Act. As a result of Native American participation in World War I, Congress grants some Native Americans
citizenship.
Meriam Report outlines the failure of previous Indian policies and
calls for reform.
Alberta Metis Organization is founded by Joseph Dion.
Indian Reorganization Act. Implements the Meriam Report recommendations, reversing many previous policies.
Johnson-O’Malley Act replaces the General Allotment Act.
Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act. Extends many of the rights provided
by the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 to Oklahoma Indian
nations.
National Congress of American Indians is founded to guard Native
American rights.
Indian Claims Commission Act. Provides a legal forum for tribes to
sue the federal government for the loss of lands.
Navajo and Hopi Rehabilitation Act is passed to assist the tribes in
developing their natural resources.
Indian Act of 1951. A new Canadian Indian Act reduces the powers
of the Indian Affairs Department but retains an assimilationist
agenda.
Public Law 280 allows greater state jurisdiction over criminal cases
involving Native Americans from California, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Nebraska (extended to Alaska Natives in 1959).
Termination Resolution. Congress initiates a policy (which continues
into the early 1960’s) of severing the federal government’s relationships with Native American nations.
Indian Health Service is transferred from the Department of the
Interior to the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.
Chicago Indian Conference, organized by anthropologist Sol Tax,
mobilizes Indian leaders to reassert their rights.
National Indian Youth Council is founded by Clyde Warrior and
others.

American Indian Tribes
Event
State of Washington rules against Native American fishing rights.
American Indian Historical Society is founded to research and teach
about Native Americans.
Hawthorn Report examines the conditions of contemporary Canadian natives and recommends that Indians be considered “citizens plus.”
American Indian Civil Rights Act guarantees reservation residents
many of the civil liberties other citizens have under the U.S.
Constitution.
American Indian Movement (AIM) is founded in Minneapolis by
Dennis Banks and Russell Means.
Canadian government’s White Paper of 1969 rejects the Hawthorn
Report’s recommendations, arguing that Canadian natives’ special status hinders their assimilation and urging the abolition of
the Indian Affairs Department and Indian Act.
Occupation of Alcatraz Island by Native American people begins
(continues through 1971).
Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act marks the beginning of the
self-determination period for Alaska Natives.
Trail of Broken Treaties Caravan proceeds to Washington, D.C., to
protest treaty violations.
Native American Rights Fund (NARF) is founded to carry Indian
issues to court.
Indian Education Act enacted; it is intended to improve the quality
of education for Native Americans (the act is revised in 1978).
Wounded Knee occupation. More than two hundred Native American activists occupy the historic site to demonstrate against oppressive Sioux reservation policies.
Navajo-Hopi Land Settlement Act facilitates negotiation between the
two nations over the disputed Joint Use Area.
Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act expands
tribal control over tribal governments and education.
Political violence increases on the Pine Ridge Reservation; two FBI
agents are killed in a shootout on June 26.
James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement is signed; Quebec Cree,
Inuit, Naskapi, and Montagnais groups cede tribal lands in exchange for money and specified hunting and fishing rights.
American Indian Policy Review Commission Report is released by
Congress, recommending that Native American nations be considered sovereign political bodies.
American Indian Freedom of Religion Act protects the rights of
Native Americans to follow traditional religious practices.
Federal Acknowledgment Program is initiated to provide guidelines
for and assist tribes seeking official recognition by the federal
government.
Indian Child Welfare Act proclaims tribal jurisdiction over child
custody decisions.

Time Line

Event
The Longest Walk, a march from Alcatraz Island to Washington,
D.C., protests government treatment of Indians.
United States v. Sioux Nation. U.S. Supreme Court upholds a $122
million judgment against the United States for illegally taking the
Black Hills.
Hopi-Navajo Joint Use Area is partitioned between the Navajo and
Hopi nations.
Canada’s Constitution Act (Constitution and Charter of Rights and
Freedoms) is passed despite the protests of Indian, Metis, and
Inuit groups.
Indian Claims Limitation Act limits the time period during which
claims can be filed against the U.S. government.
Coolican Report declares that little progress is being made to settle
Canadian native land claims.
Indian Gaming Regulatory Act officially legalizes certain types of
gambling on reservations and establishes the National Indian
Gaming Commission.
U.S. Congress approves construction of the National Museum of the
American Indian, to be part of the Smithsonian Institution.
Violence erupts on St. Regis Mohawk Reservation in dispute over
whether to allow gambling; under guard by state and federal law
enforcement officers, the tribe votes to allow gambling on the
reservation.
The U.S. Census finds the Native American population to be 1,959,234.
In Duro v. Reina, the U.S. Supreme Court holds that tribes cannot
have criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians on reservation lands.
Canada’s proposed Meech Lake Accord (amendments to the 1982
Constitution Act) is sent to defeat in Canada by native legislator
Elijah Harper; the accord provided no recognition of native rights.
Tribal Self-Governance Act extends the number of tribes involved in
the self-governance pilot project.
Native Americans protest the Columbian Quincentenary.
In a plebiscite, residents of Canada’s Northwest Territories approve
the future creation of Nunavut, a territory to be governed by the
Inuit.
The International Year of Indigenous People.
National Museum of the American Indian opens its first facility in
New York’s Heye Center (a larger museum is planned for the Mall
in Washington, D.C.).
The National Congress of American Indians and the National Black
Caucus of State Legislators ally themselves, agreeing that they
face similar political and economic forces of oppression.
Canadian minister of Indian Affairs formally apologizes to Indian
and Inuit peoples for past government atttempts to destroy native
cultures.
Eastern portion of Canada’s Northwest Territories becomes new
territory of Nunavut.

Again, a Whole Person I Have Become
Color. 19 min. 16mm.
Shenandoah Film Productions (1982)
Stresses the importance of traditional
Indian customs for Indian youth. Three
tribal elders speak of the wisdom of the
old ways; dances and ceremonies are
portrayed. Will Sampson narrates.
Age of the Buffalo
Color. 14 min. 16mm.
National Film Board of Canada (1964)
Shows how the buffalo met the needs
of the Indians for food, clothing, shelter,
and adventure, and how life changed
when the buffalo were gone.

Color. 62 min. VHS.
Library Distributors of America (1993)
Broad view of the origin and culture
of American Indians; also examines interactions between Indians and whites.

Man Came
Color. 27 min. 16mm.
Handel Film Corporation (1972)
Extensive examination of American
Indians since European discovery of the
Americas. Moves to a discussion of the
problems facing modern Indians.

Color. 50 min. VHS.

Explores the spiritual and psychological powers of masks used by Northwest Coast native peoples. Features
rarely-seen ceremonies, commentary by
spiritual leaders and relates how these
traditions were repressed by Christian
Europeans.

The Sun Dagger (Edited version)

The “dagger,” an ancient Indian celestial calendar rediscovered in 1977, is

The depictions of Indians in feature
films (often by white actors) have historically been misguided and have engendered considerable outrage. What
follows is a select list of films that provide relatively accurate portrayals of Indian life, past and present. In some of
the films all Indians are portrayed by
Indian actors; in others, white actors fill
at least some Indian roles.

Winter on an Indian Reservation
Color. 11 min. 16mm.
Inform (1973)
Shows children on a forest reservation in the Great Lakes area; provides an
intimate look at both the hardships and
joys of Indian life.
Wiping the Tears of Seven Generations
Color. 57 min. VHS.
Film Ideas (1992)
History of the Lakota people, culminating in the Bigfoot Memorial Ride, December 1990, intended to end the century of grieving since the Wounded
Knee Massacre.

Black Robe
Color. 100 min. VHS.
Samuel Goldwyn (1991)
Seventeenth century Jesuit priest is

mission. Generally accurate depiction of
early Indian-white relations as well as
intertribal Algonquin, Iroquois, and
Huron relations and warfare. From
Brian Moore’s novel. Lothaire Bluteau,
Aden Young, Sandrine Holt.

Woodland Indians of Early America

Cort (1958)
Depicts a family of hunter-culture Indians, illustrating the migratory nature
of such cultures and showing many
techniques of hunting, dress, cooking,
and home building.

Roland.
